description: Binary Horizon é uma equipe de Belém focada em desenvolver soluções criativas com dados e recursos da NASA, combinando software, análise de dados, inteligência artificial e visualização de informações. Buscamos construir um projeto tecnicamente sólido, útil e fácil de demonstrar, com foco em impacto, clareza e inovação.
summary: Amazônia Viva is a web platform that turns NASA satellite fire detections into territorial context for the Amazon. It answers the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge in two ways. First, it never adds counts from different sensors: MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) are compared only against themselves, and an experimental series converts MODIS Aqua into NOAA-20-equivalent detections, validated year by year with the uncertainty always shown. The result is a monthly fire-activity calendar for 2002–2025 that reveals seasonality, recurrence and unusual months. Second, it connects each new detection to people and places. Detections from four satellites (NOAA-20, NOAA-21, Terra, Aqua) are grouped into hotspots with public, rule-based alert levels, model wind and what lies in the path: towns, federal roads, Indigenous lands, quilombola territories and protected areas. Indigenous lands get dedicated alerts with census residents, the FUNAI office to contact and a shareable bulletin. Everything uses real, traceable public data and states its limits: it supports decisions and is not an official alert system. Pilots: Santarém and Portel (Pará, Brazil), with coverage across the nine Amazon countries.
details:
LIVE DEMO: https://amazviva.online (source code: https://github.com/filpe19/amazonia-viva)

WHAT IT DOES

Amazônia Viva is an environmental intelligence platform for the Amazon. It turns NASA satellite fire detections into context that helps people decide: where fire activity is unusual, which hotspots deserve attention, and who and what may be affected. It is built around the challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots".

HOW IT WORKS

1. Harmonized fire history. MODIS (1 km pixels, Terra/Aqua) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, NOAA-20/NOAA-21) detect fire at different resolutions, so raw counts cannot be added or compared directly. Our rule: never sum sensors. Each satellite is compared only with itself, and an experimental series converts MODIS Aqua into NOAA-20-equivalent detections. The conversion is validated by leaving one year out (for Pará: median error 14.3%, 90th percentile 54.1%, 60 active months, 2021–2025), and the uncertainty is shown on every chart. The result is a monthly fire-activity calendar for 2002–2025, with seasonal profiles, year comparison and a list of unusual months (robust z-score, P10/P90).

2. Situation center. Near-real-time FIRMS detections from four satellites are grouped into hotspots (detections within 1.5 km). Each hotspot shows its proportion (pixels, overpasses, satellites), observed displacement, model wind (Open-Meteo) and what lies within 5, 10 and 20 km or downwind: towns, federal roads (DNIT), Indigenous lands (FUNAI and OTCA), quilombola territories, settlements and protected areas. Alert levels (high, moderate, low) and detection reliability follow public, written rules; there is no arbitrary risk score, and the probability of fire reaching a place is explicitly marked as "not modeled".

3. Indigenous lands. Dedicated alerts for fire inside or within 10 km of each Indigenous land: confirmed by two or more overpasses, census residents (IBGE 2022), peoples, the FUNAI regional office to contact, nearest road and brigade, and a bulletin ready to copy or share on WhatsApp.

4. "Is it really a fire?" For each detection, the platform checks public sources: other overpasses, the FIRMS static-source type, mining titles (ANM), INPE DETER warnings and archive recurrence. It shows a reading such as "compatible with vegetation fire", "mining context" or "clearing context", with the evidence and its limits.

5. Evidence sheet. Each territory has a printable report in which every fact is labeled as observation or estimate, with its source.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Early-warning teams, civil defense, firefighters, environmental agencies, researchers and Indigenous and riverside communities get one place to see what the satellites saw and what it may mean on the ground. The goal is faster, better-informed decisions, while making clear that a detection is not a confirmed fire and that the platform does not replace official agencies. Pilots: Santarém and Portel (Pará, Brazil). In November 2026, the Pará state government declared an environmental and climate emergency. Coverage: all 144 municipalities of Pará and the nine Amazon countries.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Shapely (STRtree), pyproj, Apache Arrow/Parquet and SQLite. Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS, TanStack Query and Recharts. Quality: 93 backend tests, frontend unit tests, end-to-end tests with Playwright, 30/30 data-consistency checks against independent routes and official IBGE totals, and zero WCAG 2.1 AA violations in automated axe-core audits. The interface is available in Portuguese and English. Deployment: Docker, nginx (rate limits) and Caddy (automatic HTTPS).

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It treats sensor harmonization as a question of honesty about the data: separate series, explicit conversion and visible uncertainty. It also moves from "a dot on a map" to "a place with people", connecting every hotspot to the territories, roads and communities around it in a way that can be checked.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Data integrity (only real, traceable public data; no mock values and no estimates of affected people), clear limitations on every screen, accessibility, bilingual interface, cost (free public APIs) and responsible use: it is decision support, not an official alert system.

USE OF AI

We used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, to help write and review code, tests, data pipelines and documentation, to translate texts into English and to write the video editing scripts. whisper.cpp was used to time the subtitles. All data shown are real public data, and there are no AI-generated images, footage or voices: the videos use real screen recordings of the platform and real footage of our team member.

TEAM

Binary Horizon (Horizonte Binário): Felipe Souza (software engineer and full-stack developer), Ariel Barros (social worker) and Ronaldo Moraes (full-stack developer).

LIVE PLATFORM FOR THE LOCAL JUDGING PANEL (Portuguese and English): https://amazviva.online

dataRefs: NASA FIRMS — Fire Information for Resource Management System
NASA FIRMS Active Fire Data — VIIRS 375 m (NOAA-20, NOAA-21) and MODIS C6.1 near real time
NASA FIRMS Archive Download — MODIS and VIIRS standard processing (fire calendar 2002–2025)
NASA POWER — weather reanalysis and climatology
NASA GIBS — Global Imagery Browse Services (dated satellite basemap)
projectRefs: INPE TerraBrasilis — DETER Amazônia deforestation and degradation warnings
IBGE — territorial meshes, BC250 localities and 2022 Census
IBGE SIDRA — 2022 Census tables (Indigenous residents per land)
Censipam Panorama — Fire Panel API and GeoServer layers (FUNAI, ICMBio, CNUC, INCRA, DNIT, OTCA)
MMA CNUC — National Register of Conservation Units
OTCA — Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (Indigenous lands in other Amazon countries)
OpenFreeMap and OpenStreetMap contributors — cartographic basemap
O Liberal — news headline cited in the local-panel video (credited on screen)
Claude (Anthropic) — AI assistant used for code, documentation, translation and video editing scripts
